newsitem.title: BRAZIL: FOCUS - Confusion dogs Brazil-Mercosur import deal.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Confusion dogs Brazil-Mercosur import deal.

text.p: A deal between Brazil and its Mercosur trade bloc partners on import finance rules was dogged by contradictions on Thursday after Brazilian officials failed to agree on which countries they had included in the agreement.

Partial exemptions from the controversial new rules on short-term Brazilan import financing also turned out to be much more limited than originally presented by Brazilian Finance Minister Pedro Malan and Argentine Economy Minister Roque Fernandez.

Gustavo Franco, Central Bank Director of International Affairs, insisted in a news conference that Mercosur free trade associates Chile and Bolivia would get the same treatment as full members Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay.
That revelation surprised Foreign Ministry officials.

"I am not aware of any change (in the original decision)," said Jose Botafogo Goncalves, general sub-secretary of economic integration and foreign trade. "Mercosur consists of four countries. Chile and Bolivia are associated to it."
In the meantime, Franco's interpretaion made its way to Santiago where President Eduardo Frei said Chile would benefit from the deal thrashed out by Malan and Fernandez on Wednesday.

It was Argentina that led a barrage of angry complaints from Brazil's trading partners after Brasilia last week slapped tough limits on short-term import financing, effectively forcing imnporters to pay in cash.

The accord reached Wednesday lifted an upper limit on exemptions to $40,000 from $10,000 for Mercosur products and extended the definition of "paying in cash" for those products to 89 days from 59 days. The exemption runs for 120 days.

Only products backed by central bank Reciprocal Trade Credits (CCR), an instrument established under a Latin American trade dispute settlement agreement, are included, and only if all the conditions are met.

On Thursday it emerged that this requirement threw a huge spanner in Uruguay's prospects of enjoying the partail exemption. Though a full Mercosur member, Uruguay has not joined the trade dispute settlement mechanism that established CCRs.
Montevideo's Ambassador Mario Cesar Fernandez told Reuters his country recognized that lapse and intended to correct it.
Further confusion stemmed from differences from a presentation by Malan and Fernandez and a central bank decree drawn up on Thursday.
As presented by Malan and Fernandez, the agreement changed the definition of "paying in cash" for all Mercosur products. But Franco explained this was not the case.
In order to benefit from the exemption all the conditions have to be met, in particular the ceiling of $40,000, Franco said.

While declining to reveal government estimates of the potential impact of the Mercosur-Brazil deal, the Central Bank director contested criticism that the $40,000 limit meant only a handful of imports would benefit.
Franco said Argentine negotiators had been particularly worried about the impact Brazil's rules would have on small firms and that the limit agreed on met those concerns.
"Our measures (on import financing) are a long way from being drastic," he added.
Argentina greeted news of the accord with cautious relief.

Deputy Foreign Minister Andre Cisneros said it was "neither a win for Argentina nor a retreat for Brazil", echoing private remarks by Brazilian officials that they had not really conceded a great deal.
Cisneros added that Buenos Aires hoped there would be "no more surprises" from its giant neighbour to the north.
(-- Brasilia newsroom 55-61-2230358))
